title: Knowledge Check 6: Lessons 26-30
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 26-30 of the ai-adoption series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: According to Lesson 26, what is the core difference between an audit and continuous monitoring?
options: An audit runs continuously, while continuous monitoring is a one-time scheduled check
An audit is a scheduled, evidence-based review that checks whether controls reflect reality, while continuous monitoring watches signals all the time
An audit only applies to financial records, while continuous monitoring only applies to AI
An audit measures opinions, while continuous monitoring measures intentions
questions.explanation: The lesson defines an audit as a scheduled, evidence-based review that compares evidence to expectations, and continuous monitoring as the always-on version that watches signals the whole time. They complement each other: monitoring watches continuously, while the audit pulls back on a schedule to ask whether the lines themselves are still right.

questions.question: In the worked example, which problem best matches the kind of thing a quarterly audit catches that a real-time monitor would not?
options: A sudden security alert that triggered instantly during business hours
The firm paying for 24 unused seats on a writing assistant and a sanctioned tool gaining a new charting feature without the inventory or policy being updated
A tool that stopped working entirely and could not be reached by anyone
A vendor shutting down its API with no notice to the organization
questions.explanation: The lesson's worked example found three quiet, unglamorous gaps that no real-time signal had flagged: sixteen paid-but-unused writing-assistant seats, a finance tool whose vendor quietly added charting that was past the inventory and policy, and a coding assistant used by two people the policy did not name. These are the kind of drift a scheduled, evidence-based audit catches, not a live monitor.

questions.question: What cadence does Lesson 26 recommend as a sensible default for a typical organization?
options: Refresh the AI inventory and run evidence checks quarterly, review the full policy annually, and review high-risk systems on the quarterly cycle
Run a full audit once, never again, because AI stays the same after setup
Review everything on an annual basis only, including high-risk systems
Do not schedule audits; run them only when someone remembers to ask
questions.explanation: The lesson recommends, as a sensible default, refreshing the inventory and running evidence checks quarterly, reviewing the full policy annually, and keeping high-risk systems (anything handling client data, money, or regulated information) on the tighter quarterly cycle. It stresses that the operative requirement is a scheduled date, because a check that only happens when someone remembers is not a cadence.

questions.question: Lesson 27 explains that traditional SaaS budgeting habits break down for AI because of a structural difference. What is it?
options: AI software always costs more per user than traditional software
A large share of AI spend is usage-driven: it scales with adoption and spikes when a workflow succeeds, so it is structurally hard to forecast
AI vendors refuse to publish their prices
AI budgets are always owned by a single clean function, unlike traditional software
questions.explanation: Lesson 27 states that a large share of AI spend is usage-driven rather than seat-driven, that it scales with and often spikes when a workflow works, and that it is owned by no single function, which makes it structurally hard to forecast. The lesson describes an automation that costs nothing until it works, then costs more every month as people route work to it.

questions.question: Dhara sizes her seat bucket to active users rather than total headcount. Why does the lesson endorse this?
options: Because per-seat pricing is the most expensive model and should always be avoided

Because a headcount-sized seat plan overpays for the quiet majority, since a small slice of licensed users typically generates the bulk of AI activity while per-seat billing charges full price for everyone else
Because active users are the only people allowed to use AI under her policy
Because usage-based pricing is always cheaper than per-seat pricing at any size
questions.explanation: Lesson 27 cites the pattern that 10-20% of licensed users generate the large majority of AI activity while a per-seat contract charges full price for everyone else, and notes that past roughly a thousand users the gap between the models becomes the budget. Dhara licenses her three hundred active users instead of all eight hundred and twenty employees.

questions.question: Lesson 27 recommends start with showback and graduate to chargeback. What is the reason for that order?
options: Chargeback is more expensive to operate, so it should be saved for later
Showback creates direct financial penalty first, then chargeback adds visibility
Roughly 90% tagging coverage is required before a chargeback model can be applied fairly, so organizations build reliable attribution under showback first to avoid disputes
Chargeback is illegal until a company reaches a minimum size
questions.explanation: Lesson 27, drawing on the MLflow guide, explains that roughly 90% tagging coverage is required before a chargeback model can be applied fairly, and that below that threshold untagged costs create disputes and erode trust. So most organizations start with showback, which builds awareness through transparency without moving money, then move to chargeback once tagging is reliable.

questions.question: Lesson 28 separates leading indicators from financial outcomes. Which of these is a financial outcome a board will accept as an ROI claim?
options: Adoption rate across the organization
The number of prompts issued per user per week
Revenue uplift, cost reduction, or risk reduction attributed to the use case
Self-reported hours saved per employee
questions.explanation: Lesson 28 states that adoption rate, prompts per user, and self-reported time saved are leading indicators that show momentum but are not financial outcomes. The claims that can be defended to a board are the three outcomes a use case should connect to: revenue uplift, cost reduction, and risk reduction.

questions.question: In the worked example, Priya books about 192,000 dollars of realized benefit rather than the 384,000 dollar headline saving. Why does the lesson endorse this?
options: Because the headline saving includes licence costs that should be subtracted twice
Because finance always discounts any claim by exactly half

Because she only counts the share of saved time that became realized value, an avoided new hire and higher-quality responses, and leaves the quarter that was not actually redeployed as on-paper upside
Because she is required to underreport results until the pilot runs for a full year
questions.explanation: Lesson 28 applies the redeemed-capacity test: a saving is only realized when the freed time becomes revenue, avoided cost, or reduced risk. Priya traced where the saved time went, booked the realized half (avoided hire and higher quality) as the hard number, and logged the unredeployed quarter as upside, because counting time saved that was never reinvested is a common way a claim collapses.

questions.question: The lesson lays an AI ROI case out in four layers so a CFO can read it. Which description matches that structure?
options: Financial outcomes on top, then operational metrics, then behavioural metrics, then AI-specific health, with each layer feeding the one above it
AI-specific health on top, with financial outcomes at the base so usage is highlighted
Four separate reports with no connection between layers
A single headline ROI number with no supporting evidence
questions.explanation: Lesson 28 structures the proof as financial outcomes on top, operational metrics beneath, behavioural metrics next, and AI-specific health at the base, each layer feeding the one above it. The top layer carries the dollars and is the only one the board reads on its own, and the bottom three exist to defend it.

questions.question: A pilot succeeds, yet the use case fails when the company tries to roll it out broadly. According to Lesson 29, which set of conditions explains the most common cause of that failure?
options: The underlying model was never good enough, and the pilot team hid its errors
The pilot depended on curated data, relaxed governance with manual review, and outputs that did not act, and those support beams are removed at scale
The finance team always refuses to fund production deployments regardless of pilot results
Employees in the wider organization are inherently more resistant to change than the pilot team
questions.explanation: The lesson names the three assumptions a pilot leans on: curated data, governance applied after the fact with humans reviewing outputs, and a system that informs rather than acts. At scale those vanish, which is why Gartner finds at least 50% of generative AI projects are abandoned after proof of concept and MIT reports roughly 95% of pilots never reach measurable impact. Model quality is not the cause.

questions.question: Your support-automation pilot clears its technical checkpoints and early adoption signals. Per the four-phase pathway in Lesson 29, what is the correct next step and the gate it must clear?
options: Skip straight to full-scale rollout everywhere, because a successful pilot is proof the use case will scale

Enter an MVP phase with limited but live exposure and a gate asking whether the solution is safe and stable, whether users adopt it in a real workflow, and whether measurable operational and financial impact justifies scaling
Abandon the pilot and start a new one in a different department to test for repeatability
Move to full scale only after the vendor demonstrates better model accuracy in a benchmark
questions.explanation: The phase order is pilot, MVP, initial scaling, then full scale. The MVP puts the solution into real workflows with limited live exposure, and the decision gates ask whether the model is safe and stable, whether adoption is happening in real workflows, and whether impact justifies scaling. The lesson warns that a pilot is proof, not scale.

questions.question: Priya scales her support automation and wants the monthly review to actually decide something. Which practice from Lesson 29 makes the review a real decision mechanism rather than theater?
options: Rotating the review criteria each month so the conversation stays fresh
Naming the gate decision in advance, keeping a single shared evidence pack that tracks benefits and total cost of ownership, and using the same evidence for both finance and the AI program
Reviewing only the use cases that are clearly succeeding and skipping the rest
Letting the vendor present its own success metrics at each review
questions.explanation: The lesson says gates only work when the decision criteria are named before the project starts and the evidence pack is single and shared, so the gate meeting decides instead of becoming a dispute about data. Running AI as a managed investment means a fixed review cadence, clear stage gates, and one evidence pack that tracks both benefits and total cost of ownership.

questions.question: Lesson 30 argues that the question which separates real AI governance from theater is most fundamentally:
options: When an AI model does something it should not do, who has the authority to stop it, and does that person answer to someone who does not depend on the deployment succeeding
How many dashboards and model registries the organization has built to monitor its AI systems
Whether the AI council has a lawyers and a security officer in the room
How many policies the organization has written about responsible AI use
questions.explanation: Lesson 30 builds on the MIT Sloan Management Review argument that governance is theater when nobody can hit the stop button. The load-bearing question is who can actually stop a misbehaving model and whether that person has the standing to do it without reporting to someone who benefits from the 'yes'. Registries, dashboards, and policies are visibility infrastructure, not accountability.

questions.question: In the FinCo case, MIT CISR found that thorough governance built across all five domains backfired. Why did FinCo's program break the company?
options: Its policy took close to a year to write and was outdated on completion, a low-risk prototype took six months to approve, and frustrated teams went back to unsanctioned tools
The governance was adopted too quickly and with too little involvement from legal and compliance
The company had no AI policy at all, so employees had no rules to follow
The council reviewed every use case but never escalated anything to the executive sponsor
questions.explanation: Lesson 30 recounts the FinCo example from MIT CISR: the enterprise policy took close to a year and was outdated when finished, a low-risk agent prototype took six months to get through review, and employees needed layered sign-offs even to access the firm's own secure platform. The slowdown pushed teams back to unsanctioned tools, so shadow AI spread wider than before. This case motivates minimum viable governance.

questions.question: Which pairing captures the two design constraints Lesson 30 says an AI council most needs to survive contact with the company?
options: Decision rights plus escalation that ends in real authority, and minimum viable governance that is structurally agile and opportunity-sensitive so it does not strangle the business
A large standing membership and a fast meeting cadence so every function is always in the room
A comprehensive enterprise AI policy and a board-level committee that approves every pilot
Embedded controls in the platform and gatekeeping that requires sign-off before anyone can use an approved tool
questions.explanation: Lesson 30 pairs two ideas: real decision rights and a working escalation path (the stop authority with an independent reporting line), and minimum viable governance characterized by structural agility and opportunity sensitivity. The other options describe the failure modes the lesson warns against, including oversized bodies, over-policy, and gatekeeping that strangles adoption.
